statement: Sumerian cuneiform and Akkadian/Babylonian cuneiform are both DECIPHERED. Decipherment proceeded via Old Persian cuneiform first (Grotefend 1802 partial breakthrough on ~10 of 37 signs; Rask 1826; Burnouf and Lassen 1836; Rawlinson's copying of the trilingual Behistun Inscription 1835-1847, published 1846-1847), then Akkadian/Babylonian, publicly confirmed on 29 May 1857 when the Royal Asiatic Society sent a newly discovered Assyrian text in sealed envelopes to four scholars working independently (Rawlinson, Edward Hincks, Jules Oppert, and William Henry Fox Talbot); their translations converged closely. Sumerian, a language isolate, was recoverable chiefly via bilingual Sumerian-Akkadian lexical lists preserved by later scribes. Despite DECIPHERED status, the sign system is large and highly polyphonic, many tablets are damaged, and Sumerian as a language remains imperfectly understood in places despite the script itself being fully read.

sources.citation: Rawlinson, Henry Creswicke. The Persian Cuneiform Inscription at Behistun, Deciphered and Translated. 1846-1847.
sources.author: Henry Rawlinson

sources.citation: Account of the 29 May 1857 Royal Asiatic Society blind-translation test of Rawlinson, Hincks, Oppert, and Fox Talbot on a Tiglath-Pileser I prism text.

notes: Exact Rawlinson Behistun publication date(s) split 1846/1847/1849 across sources, likely reflecting multi-part publication — flagged, not fully resolved.
